archetype.name: Cup Contender (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A team that controls play at 5-on-5 and has the best power play in the league, good enough to win at a contender's rate even though its goaltending has been below average.

report.headline: Elite shot control and a lethal power play, held back by its goaltending
report.take:
Nine games in, Utah looks like a team that has taken a real step, and the record undersells how one-sided its hockey has been. The Mammoth own 56.8% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (4th) and 56% of the shot attempts (4th). They allow 19.3 shots a game, the fewest in the league and seven fewer than the league average. The roster grades say the same thing: an A forward group and an A+ blueline, led by Mikhail Sergachev, third of 242 on the defense tab with 10 points in 22-plus minutes a night.

The record isn't built on luck. Pts vs Goal Diff sits at 0.2, mid-pack, so Utah isn't stealing close games, and 5-on-5 PDO is 99, a shade below average. What the PDO average hides is a split: the skaters shoot 12.1% in all situations (10th), while the goalies stop only 87.9% (22nd). Goalies GSAx is -3.6 (25th). That is why a team that barely lets opponents shoot still gives up 3.0 goals a game, 11th in the league rather than near the top. The power play at 35.3%, first in the league and nearly 15 points above average, covers for a penalty kill at 73.3% (25th).

The last five games show the risk. Utah went 3-2, but it lost 1-6 in Boston and 2-6 at home to Edmonton and allowed 3.8 goals a game, 0.8 above its season rate. With shots against this low, that is mostly the goaltending again. The forward scoring also leans on the power play. Nick Schmaltz and Clayton Keller each have 11 points, but both sit below 50% in 5-on-5 expected goals, while Barrett Hayton (70.7%) and Anders Lee (63.6%) drive play from lower in the lineup.

Last season's history argues the goaltending should improve. In 2025-26 the goalies were +14.1 GSAx, and the team finished 43-33-6 despite -9.2 Pts vs Goal Diff, a club that was better than its record. The shot suppression is new and looks structural. If Karel Vejmelka returns to anything like last year's team level, Utah's goals against should fall to match its shots against, and this becomes one of the best teams in the West. The power play will cool, so the steady part of the case is the 5-on-5 game.

strengths.title: Suffocating 5-on-5 shot suppression
strengths.body: Utah allows the fewest shots on goal in the league and wins the expected-goals battle by a wide margin. An A+ blueline that moves the puck, with Sergachev on top and Weegar, Schmidt and Marino all above 59% in expected goals, keeps play in the other end. This is the most repeatable part of a hot start, because shot rates settle faster than shooting or save percentages.

strengths.title: League-best power play
strengths.body: At 35.3%, the power play is first in the league and far above the 20.4% average. Keller, Cooley and Guenther each have six or seven power-play points. No unit holds that rate over a season, but last year's 20% suggests this group has gotten genuinely better, and some of the gain should stick even after it regresses.

strengths.title: Depth forwards driving play
strengths.body: The lower lines are winning their minutes. Hayton holds 70.7% of the expected goals and Lee 63.6%, both well above the top-line scorers. That depth is a big part of why the team share stays high when the stars are only breaking even at 5-on-5.

concerns.title: Goaltending giving goals back
concerns.body: The goalies are saving 87.9% against a league average of 89.3%, and they are 3.6 goals below expected. Vejmelka carries most of the starts at .879 and -2.1 GSAx. That is the gap between Utah's shot numbers and its goals against. The goalies were +14.1 GSAx last season, so improvement is likely, but it remains the biggest variable in the season.

concerns.title: A leaky penalty kill
concerns.body: The kill is at 73.3%, 25th and well below the 79% league average, and it was 78.1% last season. With so few shots allowed at even strength, special-teams goals against become a large part of what beats this team. Improvement is possible, but it depends partly on the same goaltending.

concerns.title: Recent goals-against spike
concerns.body: Over the last five games Utah allowed 3.8 a game and was outscored, including 6-goal losses to Boston and Edmonton. It is a small sample, but it points the same way as the save-percentage problem rather than a collapse in structure.

trend.note: A 3-game win streak and a strong opening stretch gave way to a choppier last five, with two lopsided losses. The underlying shot control has held throughout, so the wobble reads as goaltending variance, not decline.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, two soft spots, then two real tests
weekAhead.body:
Pittsburgh visits first, and the Penguins are 25th on the site with D-graded goaltending and the league's 31st-ranked defense against wingers. That suits Keller and Guenther. Seattle at home looks good on paper at 5-3-1 and 5th in offense, but its 42% shot-attempt share (29th) and 105.3 PDO describe a team being outplayed and riding its shooting. Utah's possession game should tilt that one heavily.

The back half is harder. Tampa Bay matches Utah in play-driving (58.9% xGF, 2nd), but its power play is 30th, which shields Utah's weak kill. Minnesota leads the Central and is the real measuring stick. The Wild kill 89.3% of penalties, save 92.2% of shots and hold wingers well under expectation, so Utah's power play and wing scorers face their stiffest test of the season.

keyMatchups.title: Utah wingers against Pittsburgh's defense
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh gives wingers more than a point a game above their usual output, 31st in the league. With Keller and Guenther driving the power play and Pittsburgh's goaltending graded D, this is the best scoring chance of the week.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's shooting luck against Utah's suppression
keyMatchups.body: The Kraken are 30th in shots allowed and 29th in shot share, propped up by a 105.3 PDO. Utah's league-best shot suppression should starve them, as long as the goaltending stops the few shots that get through.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's power play against Minnesota's kill
keyMatchups.body: The league's best power play meets a 4th-ranked penalty kill backed by a .922 save percentage. Minnesota's own 32.1% power play also threatens Utah's 25th-ranked kill, so special teams likely decide the division game.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Vejmelka's save percentage climbs toward the league average. If it does, Utah's goals against finally matches its shots against.

restOfSeason.body:
The pace numbers (55 wins, 109 points) are an early-season sample, but the profile behind them is sturdy. Utah leads the league in shot suppression, sits top-four in both possession shares and grades A or better at forward and on defense. The power play will fall from 35% and the skaters' shooting may cool slightly, so expect fewer goals than the current 3.67 a game. Goals against should drift down, though, if the goaltending gets anywhere near last season's level. A team this dominant at 5-on-5 rarely stays at a .879 save percentage.

I'd project roughly 98 to 108 points, comfortably a playoff team and in the mix for the Central lead with Minnesota and Colorado. The ceiling is higher if Vejmelka stabilizes. The floor drops toward the low 90s only if the goaltending stays near the bottom of the league and the kill doesn't improve.
swingFactors: How far the power play regresses

confidence.note: Nine games is a small sample, but possession and shot data stabilize early and they agree with the grades.
